title: What the Instrument Actually Sees
scopeNote: This keeps the instruments, the judgement about what each directly observes, and the three-part analysis that follows it. The informant-report instrument, which sits at a level between the individual and the institutional, the prediction round and the closing claims exercise are in the longer version, and the synthesis names the missing level.
summary: Four instruments all published as measurements of prejudice. Each directly observes something much narrower, and the fourth is not a measure of individuals at all.
learningObjectives: Say what each instrument directly observes before anything is inferred.
Distinguish an observation from the inference usually reported with it.
Recognise that measures at different levels are about different objects.
Explain why no study of individual attitudes can confirm or refute an institutional pattern.
Say where an instrument stops being evidence about a construct and becomes the construct.
interactionTypes: a judgement about what differs between four instruments
four instruments opened one at a time
one judgement per instrument before its analysis is shown
the inference, the alternatives and the limits shown together
a four-way comparison of level, observation and limit
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No task on the page measures anything about the reader and the reader never takes any of the instruments described.
dataStatus: Vantry, the Uplands and the Lowlands are invented. No group in them stands for any real group anywhere, no stereotype content appears at all, no figure is a prevalence estimate, a norm or a published effect, and every number was written for teaching.
contentNote: The subject is how prejudice is measured rather than prejudice itself. The activity turns on what an instrument records, and it would run identically for any pair of invented categories; no attitude, belief or stereotype content is presented or enacted anywhere.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout. The instrument is a group of native radio buttons in a labelled fieldset, and the judgement is a choice grid whose options carry three non-colour state signals plus a visually hidden sentence naming the state; once answered they are locked with aria-disabled rather than the disabled attribute so they stay reachable and readable. The comparison is a real table with row and column headers and every cell is a sentence. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: For each instrument the correct description is always the deflationary one, and the distractors are not straw men: each is a description somebody publishes, and the feedback names a wrong choice as the inference rather than the observation while crediting the unchosen ones as things that get written. The payoff is the levels point. Three instruments are about an individual and the fourth is a distribution across an organisation over twelve years, and its limits run in both directions: it does not establish that any individual acted on a prejudice, and no study of individual attitudes, however large, can confirm or refute it, because the two are claims about different objects. One implementation defect found and fixed during construction, which also affected the paired crowd activity: calling setAttribute with null writes the literal string null into the markup rather than omitting the attribute, so table rows without a state were shipping a meaningless data-state of null. Both now set the attribute only when there is a state, and the test suite checks for the string specifically.
readmeTopic: what a measure of prejudice records, and how far that is from what it is called
